Mod
MOD
noun / adjective (Boomer slang)
Short for modern or modernist, originally the London youths of the late 1950s who loved modern jazz. By the early 1960s the Mods were a British subculture of sharp tailored suits, parkas, Italian scooters, soul and R&B, and pills, famous for their seaside brawls with the leather-clad Rockers at Clacton, Margate, and Brighton in 1964; the Who were their band. In America mod came to mean the whole "Swinging London" look of 1965–67 — Carnaby Street, Mary Quant’s miniskirt, Twiggy, op-art prints.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A Mod was a fashion-obsessed British youth of the early 1960s — immaculate suits, scooters with a dozen mirrors, all-night dancing — and in America mod meant anything in the Swinging London style: miniskirts, geometric prints, white boots. "That dress is so mod." The Christian observation: the Mod subculture made fashion a religion of the young, and its rivalry with the Rockers made it a tribe. Both are old temptations. Paul writes, "Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26) — a fair description of two gangs of teenagers fighting on Brighton beach over hairstyles and music. The deeper issue is identity. The Mod was what he wore. Scripture locates a person’s worth elsewhere: "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:3–4). And the mod style’s most famous product, the miniskirt, raises a question every Christian family still faces: Paul’s call for "modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9). The 1828 word modest sits right beside mod in the dictionary, and the two make a useful pair: one is what the world calls up to date, the other what God calls becoming. "Be not conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2) does not require looking old-fashioned; it requires that fashion never sit on the throne.

Webster 1828 Definition

Early-1960s British youth subculture (from modern) of sharp suits, scooters, and soul; in America, the Swinging London style of 1965–67 — fashion as identity and tribe, set by Scripture against the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4) and modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).

MOD, n. (British, late 1950s–60s; Boomer era) A member of a youth subculture devoted to sharp modern fashion, scooters, and soul / R&B music, rivals of the Rockers. adj. (US, 1965–67) In the bold, youthful London style; fashionable, up to date. "A mod dress."

Webster (1828) — MODERN, adjective [Latin modo, and ern, which we find in other Latin words that have reference to time, as in hodiernus, hesternus.] 1. Pertaining to the present time, or time not long past; late; recent; not ancient or remote in past time; as modern days, ages or time; modern authors; modern fashions; modern taste; modern practice. 2. Common; mean; vulgar. [ Not used .]

Decode for families: mod and modest share nothing but letters — and a useful conversation.

Key Scripture

1Pe 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

Gal 5:26 — "Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another."

Rom 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

Modern Corruption

Mod culture made fashion the self and style a tribe; Scripture places worth in the hidden man of the heart and asks for apparel that is modest, not merely modern.

expand to see more

The Mods were the first youth subculture built almost entirely on consumption. To be a Mod was to buy the right suit, the right scooter, the right records, and to spend every penny of a working-class wage on looking sharp. The Rockers defined themselves the same way with leather and motorcycles. When the two tribes fought on the beaches in 1964, the newspapers were shocked; Paul would not have been (Gal 5:26). Identity sought in things is always fragile, and fragile identities fight.

The mod style that crossed the Atlantic brought the miniskirt, and with it a revolution in what was considered acceptable for women to wear. A Christian family need not be stuck in 1955 to see that 1Ti 2:9 still speaks. Modesty is not a fashion; it is a disposition of the heart toward God and neighbor that shows itself in dress. The modern question is always the same as the ancient one: who am I dressing for?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin modo (just now) → modernus → English modern → late-1950s London modernist (jazz fan) → 1960s Mod subculture → US mod (fashionable, 1965–67).

Latin modo — just now; modernus — of the present time

English modern — of the present age; new-fashioned (1828: "late; recent")

Late 1950s London: modernists — fans of modern jazz

1964: Mods and Rockers clash at Clacton, Margate, Brighton

1965–67 US: mod — Carnaby Street / Swinging London style
